position: both — *a teal sweater*; *the walls are teal*
form: from the name of the duck, which has a band of this color on its head

senses.gloss: Of a dark blue-green color.
examples: She painted the kitchen cabinets *teal*.
He showed up in a *teal* tie and gray pants.
The team's new uniforms are *teal* and black.

position: both — *a tearful goodbye*; *she was tearful all morning*

senses.gloss: Crying, or close to crying.
examples: They said a *tearful* goodbye at the gate.
She got *tearful* when she talked about her father.
His speech was more *tearful* than anyone expected.

position: both — *teary eyes*; *I always get teary at weddings*

senses.gloss: Having tears in the eyes.
examples: The ending of that movie makes me *teary* every time.
She looked up with *teary* eyes.
Dad got a little *teary* during the toast.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *she got teary-eyed*; before a noun: *a teary-eyed crowd*

senses.gloss: With tears in the eyes, usually from strong feeling.
examples: Half the room was *teary-eyed* by the end of the ceremony.
He gets *teary-eyed* whenever that song comes on.
A *teary-eyed* fan handed her a bouquet.

position: both — *a teasing smile*; *his tone was teasing*

senses.gloss: Making fun of someone in a friendly, playful way.
examples: She said it in a *teasing* voice, so nobody took it badly.
He gave his sister a *teasing* look.
Their whole conversation was light and *teasing*.

position: both — *a technical problem*; *the report gets technical*

senses.gloss: Relating to the machines, methods and skills of a particular field.
examples: The site is down because of a *technical* problem.
She has the *technical* skills for the job.
*Technical* support finally called me back.

senses.gloss: Needing special knowledge to follow.
examples: The paper gets very *technical* after page ten.
Can you explain it in less *technical* language?

senses.gloss: True only by a strict reading of the rules.
examples: It was a *technical* violation, but the referee let it go.
He won the fight by *technical* knockout.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *technological change*

senses.gloss: Relating to technology and the changes it brings.
examples: *Technological* change has hit that industry hard.
The company made a big *technological* leap in two years.
We teach students to keep up with *technological* tools.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *tectonic plates*

senses.gloss: Relating to the huge plates that make up the earth's crust.
examples: The earthquake happened where two *tectonic* plates meet.
*Tectonic* activity built these mountains.
Geologists study *tectonic* movement along the fault.

senses.gloss: So large that it changes everything, like the movement of the earth.
examples: The election marked a *tectonic* shift in the country's politics.
Streaming caused a *tectonic* change in how music is sold.

position: both — *a tedious meeting*; *the drive was tedious*

senses.gloss: Boring because it is long and repetitive.
examples: Copying the numbers by hand is *tedious* work.
The meeting was even more *tedious* than the last one.
It's a *tedious* drive, but the road is easy.

position: both — *teeming streets*; *the pond is teeming with frogs*
form: -ing from *teem*, a verb almost never met without *with*

senses.gloss: Full of living things that move around.
examples: The pond is *teeming* with tadpoles in May.
We walked through the *teeming* streets of the old city.
The reef was *teeming* with fish.

position: attributive only — *teen movies*; after a verb say *a teenager* or *teenage*
contrast: *a teen* is also a noun, a person from 13 to 19; *her teens* are those years: *She learned to drive in her teens*.

senses.gloss: Made for or done by people aged 13 to 19.
examples: He writes *teen* novels that sell by the millions.
The magazine covers *teen* fashion.
*Teen* drivers pay more for insurance.

position: attributive only — *a teenage son*; after a verb say *is a teenager*

senses.gloss: Aged between 13 and 19, or belonging to that age.
examples: They have two *teenage* sons.
*Teenage* boys eat an unbelievable amount of food.
She remembers her *teenage* years with mixed feelings.

position: attributive only — *their teenaged daughter*
contrast: *teenage* and *teenaged* mean exactly the same thing; *teenage* is much more common in American writing.

senses.gloss: Aged between 13 and 19.
examples: Their *teenaged* daughter watched the younger kids.
A group of *teenaged* volunteers cleaned up the park.
He was a *teenaged* runner with Olympic hopes.

position: both — *a teensy apartment*; *the portions are teensy*
form: a playful form of *teeny*, often doubled: *teensy-weensy*
contrast: Very informal and often childlike; in writing use *tiny*.

senses.gloss: Extremely small.
examples: The soup needs a *teensy* bit more salt.
Her studio is even *teensier* than mine.
They served the cake in *teensy* squares.

position: both — *a teeny bug*; *the print is teeny*

senses.gloss: Very small.
examples: There's a *teeny* hole in this sock.
The print on the label is the *teeniest* I've ever seen.
She keeps a *teeny* notebook in her pocket.

position: both — *telepathic powers*; *those twins are practically telepathic*

senses.gloss: Able to send or receive thoughts without speaking.
examples: In the book the aliens are *telepathic*.
She claims she has *telepathic* powers.
Those two are so close they seem *telepathic*.

position: both — *a telling detail*; *his silence was telling*

senses.gloss: Showing the truth about something without meaning to.
examples: The most *telling* detail was the empty parking lot.
Her long pause was *telling*.
It's *telling* that nobody from management showed up.

position: attributive only — *the telltale signs*

senses.gloss: Showing clearly that something is there, especially something hidden.
examples: The *telltale* smell of smoke was coming from the kitchen.
Doctors look for the *telltale* signs of the disease.
There were *telltale* scratches around the lock.

position: both — *a temperamental chef*; *the printer is temperamental*
contrast: Not the Russian 'темпераментный' in the sense of lively or passionate; in English it means moody and hard to deal with.

senses.gloss: Changing mood suddenly and often.
examples: The chef is brilliant but *temperamental*.
He got more *temperamental* as the deadline got closer.
She's not *temperamental*; she just says what she thinks.

senses.gloss: Working well one day and badly the next.
examples: The old printer is *temperamental* in humid weather.
Our car is *temperamental* on cold mornings.

position: both — *a temperate climate*; *the winters here are temperate*
contrast: Don't confuse it with *temporary*, which is about time, or with *temperamental*.

senses.gloss: Never very hot and never very cold.
examples: Oregon has a *temperate* climate near the coast.
These plants grow best in *temperate* regions.
Winters in the valley are more *temperate* than in the mountains.

senses.gloss: Calm and controlled in what you say or do.
examples: Her response to the criticism was *temperate* and careful.
He is *temperate* in everything, from food to spending.

position: both — *tempered glass*; *the glass is tempered*
contrast: Most often met inside compounds: *even-tempered*, *bad-tempered*, *hot-tempered*, where it means 'having that kind of temper'.

senses.gloss: Made harder and stronger by heating and then cooling.
examples: The shower door is made of *tempered* glass.
A *tempered* steel blade holds its edge.
Car windows are *tempered* so they break into small pieces.

senses.gloss: Made less extreme by something else.
examples: He gave a *tempered* response instead of firing back.
The report shows a *tempered* optimism about next year.

position: both — *a tempestuous marriage*; *their friendship was tempestuous*
form: -ous from *tempest*, an old word for a violent storm

senses.gloss: Full of strong feeling, arguments and sudden changes.
examples: They had a *tempestuous* marriage that lasted forty years.
The band's *tempestuous* early years are all in the documentary.
Her relationship with the director was more *tempestuous* than anyone knew.

position: attributive only — *the temporal order of events*
contrast: *temporal* means 'having to do with time'; *temporary* means 'lasting only a short while'. A *temporal* arrangement is one in time, not a short-term one.

senses.gloss: Relating to time or to the order of events in time.
examples: The novel plays with the *temporal* order of events.
We looked for a *temporal* link between the two accidents.
Physicists talk about spatial and *temporal* dimensions.

senses.gloss: Belonging to this world rather than to religion.
examples: The church lost most of its *temporal* power.
He drew a line between *temporal* and spiritual authority.

position: both — *a temporary job*; *the fix is temporary*
contrast: Not the same as *temporal*, which means 'relating to time'.

senses.gloss: Lasting for a limited time only.
examples: She took a *temporary* job over the summer.
This is a *temporary* fix until the part arrives.
The road closure is *temporary*.

position: both — *a tempting offer*; *that sounds tempting*
form: -ing from *tempt* — what makes you want something

senses.gloss: Making you want to have or do something.
examples: They made him a *tempting* offer.
It's *tempting* to skip the meeting and go home.
A quiet weekend sounds more *tempting* every year.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *that position is no longer tenable*
contrast: The negative *untenable* is far more common: *an untenable position*.

senses.gloss: Able to be defended against criticism or attack.
examples: After the report came out, his story was barely *tenable*.
Is that reading of the law still *tenable*?
They looked for a more *tenable* compromise.

position: both — *a tenacious reporter*; *she is tenacious*

senses.gloss: Not giving up, even when something is hard.
examples: She's the most *tenacious* reporter on the staff.
It took a *tenacious* defense to win that game.
He was *tenacious* about getting the records released.

senses.gloss: Holding on tightly and hard to get rid of.
examples: The weed has a *tenacious* root system.
That cough is *tenacious* — it's been three weeks.

position: both — *a tendentious article*; *the summary is tendentious*

senses.gloss: Written or said to push one opinion, not to be fair.
examples: The article is well written but deeply *tendentious*.
He gave a *tendentious* summary of what the study found.
Her second book is even more *tendentious* than the first.

position: both — *a tender look*; *the meat is tender*
contrast: *tender* is also a verb (*tender your resignation*) and a noun (*legal tender*). The phrase *at a tender age* means 'very young'.

senses.gloss: Gentle, kind and loving.
examples: He gave her a *tender* look across the table.
There's a *tender* moment near the end of the film.
She spoke to the child in a *tender* voice.

senses.gloss: Soft and easy to cut or chew.
examples: Cook the beans until they're *tender*.
This roast came out *more tender* than last time.

senses.gloss: Sore and painful when touched.
examples: My ankle is still *tender* where I twisted it.
The doctor asked if the area was *tender*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *tenderized steak*

senses.gloss: Made softer by pounding, cutting or soaking in a marinade.
examples: The recipe calls for *tenderized* cutlets.
He fried up a piece of *tenderized* steak.
The meat is already *tenderized*, so it cooks fast.

position: attributive only — *a tenfold increase*
contrast: After a verb the same word is an adverb: *Sales rose tenfold* — not *were tenfold*.

senses.gloss: Ten times as big or as many.
examples: The city saw a *tenfold* increase in applications.
A *tenfold* jump in cases forced the schools to close.
They promised a *tenfold* return on the investment.

position: both — *a tense meeting*; *everyone was tense*
contrast: *tense* is also a noun in grammar: *the past tense*.

senses.gloss: Nervous and unable to relax.
examples: She gets *tense* before every flight.
He looked *tense* all through dinner.
I was *more tense* about the interview than about the test.

senses.gloss: Full of worry, so that nobody feels comfortable.
examples: It was a *tense* meeting, and it ran two hours.
The room went *tense* when he walked in.

senses.gloss: Stretched tight and stiff.
examples: My shoulders are *tense* from driving all day.
Her jaw was *tense*.

position: both — *a tentative date*; *the plan is tentative*

senses.gloss: Not final, and likely to change.
examples: We have a *tentative* date for the wedding.
The two sides reached a *tentative* agreement.
The schedule is *tentative* until the permits come through.

senses.gloss: Done without confidence, as if you might stop at any moment.
examples: He took a few *tentative* steps on the bad knee.
Her answer was *tentative*, almost a question.

position: both — *a tenuous connection*; *the link is tenuous*

senses.gloss: So weak or thin that it could easily fail or be wrong.
examples: The connection between the two cases is *tenuous* at best.
He has a *tenuous* hold on his job.
Their evidence looks more *tenuous* every week.

position: both — *a tenured professor*; *she is tenured*
form: -ed from the noun *tenure*, a permanent university post

senses.gloss: Holding a permanent teaching position that cannot easily be taken away.
examples: She became a *tenured* professor at thirty-six.
Only *tenured* faculty vote on that committee.
He's *tenured* now, so he can take the risky project.

position: both — *tepid coffee*; *the water is tepid*

senses.gloss: Only slightly warm, when it should be hot or cold.
examples: The coffee had gone *tepid*.
Wash the sweater in *tepid* water.
He drank the *tepid* soup without complaining.

senses.gloss: Showing very little interest or enthusiasm.
examples: The new album got a *tepid* review.
Her response to the idea was *tepid*.

position: both — *terminal cancer*; *his illness is terminal*
contrast: *a terminal* is also a noun: an airport building or a computer screen.

senses.gloss: Certain to cause death, and in its last stage.
examples: He was diagnosed with *terminal* cancer in March.
The hospice cares for *terminal* patients.
Her illness is *terminal*, but she is still working.

senses.gloss: At the end of a line, route or process.
examples: The *terminal* station is two stops past downtown.
Cut the stem above the *terminal* bud.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *terrestrial animals*

senses.gloss: Living on land rather than in water or in trees.
examples: Tortoises are *terrestrial* animals.
The island has very few *terrestrial* predators.
These orchids are *terrestrial*, not the kind that grow on branches.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the earth rather than to space.
examples: Mars and Venus are *terrestrial* planets.
The signal turned out to have a *terrestrial* source.

position: both — *a terrific dinner*; *the show was terrific*
contrast: A trap: although it comes from the same root as *terror*, *terrific* is a compliment. The frightening word is *terrifying*.

senses.gloss: Very good; excellent.
examples: She did a *terrific* job on the presentation.
We had a *terrific* time in Chicago.
That's a *terrific* idea.

senses.gloss: Very great in size, force or degree.
examples: There was a *terrific* crash from the garage.
The engine puts out a *terrific* amount of heat.

position: both — *a territorial dispute*; *cats are territorial*

senses.gloss: Relating to the land a country or state controls.
examples: The two countries have a long *territorial* dispute.
Fishing boats stayed outside *territorial* waters.
The treaty settled their *territorial* claims.

senses.gloss: Ready to defend your own space or area from others.
examples: Male robins are very *territorial* in the spring.
He's *territorial* about the kitchen when he cooks.

position: both — *terror-stricken passengers*; *the children were terror-stricken*

senses.gloss: Filled with sudden, overwhelming fear.
examples: *Terror-stricken* passengers ran for the exits.
She stood *terror-stricken* in the doorway.
The dog was *terror-stricken* by the fireworks.

position: both — *a terse reply*; *his answer was terse*
contrast: *terse* is short in a way that sounds unfriendly; *concise* is short in a way that is praised.

senses.gloss: Using very few words, in a way that sounds cold or annoyed.
examples: He sent a *terse* two-line reply.
Her second email was even *terser* than the first.
The coach was *terse* with reporters after the loss.

position: attributive only — *a tertiary source*

senses.gloss: Third in order or importance, after the first two.
examples: An encyclopedia is a *tertiary* source.
Patients are sent to a *tertiary* care center for surgery.
Tourism is a *tertiary* concern for the town budget.

position: attributive only — *testicular cancer*

senses.gloss: Relating to the testicles.
examples: *Testicular* cancer is very treatable when it's caught early.
The clinic teaches men how to do a *testicular* self-exam.
He was treated for a *testicular* injury.

position: both — *a testy exchange*; *he gets testy when he's hungry*

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed and quick to answer sharply.
examples: He gets *testy* when he hasn't eaten.
There was a *testy* exchange between the two senators.
She was *testier* than usual after the long flight.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *Teutonic efficiency*
comparison: not gradable — but *very Teutonic* when it means 'typical of Germans'
contrast: Outside history books it is usually half-joking, about German thoroughness or seriousness.

senses.gloss: Relating to the ancient Germanic peoples, or to Germans and what is seen as their character.
examples: The trains run with *Teutonic* precision.
He studies the *Teutonic* tribes of the Roman period.
There's something very *Teutonic* about the way the office is organized.

position: both — *Texan hospitality*; *his accent is unmistakably Texan*
comparison: not gradable — but *very Texan* when it means 'typical of Texas'
contrast: *a Texan* is also a noun, a person from Texas. Before many nouns Americans use *Texas* itself: *Texas barbecue*, *the Texas heat*.

senses.gloss: From the state of Texas, or typical of it.
examples: We were met with *Texan* hospitality.
His accent is unmistakably *Texan*.
The menu is *Texan* down to the last brisket.

position: attributive only — *a textbook example*
contrast: The noun *a textbook* is a book for a course. As an adjective the word always means 'exactly like the standard example', and it goes only before a noun.

senses.gloss: Matching the standard example of something perfectly.
examples: That was a *textbook* landing.
The case is a *textbook* example of how not to run a company.
She made a *textbook* tackle.

position: attributive only — *textual evidence*

senses.gloss: Relating to a written text and its exact words.
examples: Back up your claim with *textual* evidence.
The editor made a few small *textual* changes.
Scholars compared the *textual* differences between the two manuscripts.

position: both — *a textured wall*; *the paper is textured*

senses.gloss: Having a surface you can feel, not flat and smooth.
examples: The invitations are printed on *textured* paper.
We put in a *textured* floor so it wouldn't be slippery.
The ceiling is *textured*, which makes it hard to paint.

senses.gloss: Made of many layers or details that are worth noticing.
examples: Her new album has a richer, more *textured* sound.
The novel gives us a *textured* picture of small-town life.

position: both — *Thai food*; *the recipe is Thai*
comparison: not gradable — but *very Thai* when it means 'typical of Thailand'
contrast: *Thai* is also a noun: the language, and a person from Thailand.

senses.gloss: From Thailand, or relating to Thailand and its people.
examples: We ordered *Thai* food for dinner.
She's taking *Thai* cooking classes.
The dish is sweet, sour and hot, which is very *Thai*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a thankless job*; *the work is thankless*
contrast: It describes the work, not the person. A person who gives no thanks is *ungrateful*.

senses.gloss: Hard to do and never appreciated by anyone.
senses.ru: неблагодарный, за который не скажут спасибо
examples: Being the referee is a *thankless* job.
She took on the *thankless* task of sorting the files.
Cleaning up after a party is *thankless* work.

position: both — *a theatrical production*; *his reaction was theatrical*

senses.gloss: Relating to the theater and to acting.
examples: The film got a *theatrical* release in June.
She works in *theatrical* lighting.
The school has a strong *theatrical* tradition.

senses.gloss: Exaggerated and done to be noticed.
examples: He gave a *theatrical* sigh and left the room.
Her apology was *theatrical* and nobody believed it.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *thematic units*

senses.gloss: Organized around a subject or theme, or relating to one.
examples: The course is broken into *thematic* units.
There's a clear *thematic* link between the two novels.
The museum arranged the show in *thematic* rooms.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a theocratic state*

senses.gloss: Governed by religious leaders or by religious law.
examples: The country became a *theocratic* state after the revolution.
He compared the group's rules to a *theocratic* system.
*Theocratic* governments answer to clerics, not to voters.

position: attributive only — *a theological argument*

senses.gloss: Relating to the study of religion and of God.
examples: He teaches at a *theological* seminary.
The split began as a *theological* argument about baptism.
She wrote her thesis on a *theological* question from the Middle Ages.

position: both — *theoretical physics*; *the risk is purely theoretical*

senses.gloss: Based on ideas and theory rather than on practice.
examples: She works in *theoretical* physics.
The course is *theoretical*, with no lab work.
There's a big gap between the *theoretical* model and the shop floor.

senses.gloss: Possible in principle but not happening in reality.
examples: For most people the danger is purely *theoretical*.
He raised a *theoretical* objection that nobody could test.

position: both — *therapeutic exercises*; *I find gardening therapeutic*

senses.gloss: Used to treat an illness or injury.
examples: The drug has a narrow *therapeutic* range.
He was given *therapeutic* exercises for his back.
The state allows *therapeutic* use of the plant.

senses.gloss: Making you feel calmer and better, even if it isn't medicine.
examples: I find weeding the garden oddly *therapeutic*.
A long walk is more *therapeutic* than an hour online.

position: attributive only — *thermal energy*, *thermal socks*
contrast: *thermals* is also a noun: warm underwear worn under your clothes.

senses.gloss: Relating to heat.
examples: The camera picks up the *thermal* signature of the engine.
The plant turns *thermal* energy into electricity.
We checked the windows for *thermal* leaks.

senses.gloss: Made to keep body heat in.
examples: Pack *thermal* socks for the hike.
He sleeps in a *thermal* shirt all winter.

position: attributive only — *a thermonuclear weapon*

senses.gloss: Using the huge energy released when light atoms join at very high temperature.
examples: The country tested its first *thermonuclear* device in 1952.
A *thermonuclear* weapon is far more powerful than an atomic bomb.
The sun runs on *thermonuclear* fusion.

position: both — *a thick book*; *the walls are thick*
contrast: For people and animals use *fat*, not *thick*: a *thick* person sounds like an insult meaning 'slow to understand'.

senses.gloss: Having a large distance between one surface and the opposite one.
examples: He handed me a *thick* envelope.
The walls are two feet *thick*.
Use the *thicker* board for the shelf.

senses.gloss: Not flowing easily, like a heavy liquid.
examples: The gravy is too *thick* — add a little water.
She likes her milkshakes *thick*.

senses.gloss: Made of many things growing or packed close together.
examples: A *thick* fog rolled in off the bay.
He has *thick* dark hair.
We cut a path through the *thick* brush.

senses.gloss: Strong and easy to hear, of an accent.
examples: She speaks with a *thick* Boston accent.
His English is good, but the accent is *thick*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *you have to be thick-skinned*; also *a thick-skinned politician*

senses.gloss: Not easily hurt by criticism or insults.
examples: You have to be *thick-skinned* to work in this business.
He's *thick-skinned* enough to laugh off the comments.
Reporters need a *thick-skinned* editor.

position: attributive only — *those thieving raccoons*
contrast: Informal and usually half-joking, most often about animals or about someone taking small things.

senses.gloss: In the habit of stealing.
examples: Those *thieving* raccoons got into the trash again.
He called his brother a *thieving* little rat.
*Thieving* gulls circled over the picnic tables.

position: both — *a thin-skinned boss*; *he's too thin-skinned for this job*

senses.gloss: Easily hurt or offended by criticism.
examples: He's too *thin-skinned* to read his own reviews.
A *thin-skinned* manager makes everyone careful.
She gets *thin-skinned* when she's tired.

position: both — *a third-rate hotel*; *the food was third-rate*

senses.gloss: Of very poor quality.
examples: We stayed in a *third-rate* hotel near the airport.
The script is *third-rate*, but the acting saves it.
He gave a *third-rate* imitation of the original.

position: attributive only — *a third-year student*

senses.gloss: In the third year of a course, a job or a program.
examples: She's a *third-year* law student.
The hospital hired two *third-year* residents.
He's in his *third-year* slump as a starter.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I'm thirsty*; before a noun: *thirsty hikers*
contrast: English says *I'm thirsty*, never *I have thirst* — the state is an adjective, as with *hungry* and *tired*.

senses.gloss: Needing or wanting something to drink.
examples: I'm *thirsty* — is there any water left?
The salty popcorn made everyone *thirstier*.
They handed out lemonade to the *thirsty* runners.

senses.gloss: Wanting something very much.
examples: The team was *thirsty* for a win after four losses.
He's *thirsty* for any news from home.

position: both — *a thorny issue*; *the bush is thorny*

senses.gloss: Difficult and full of problems.
examples: Pensions are the *thorniest* issue in the negotiation.
They avoided the *thorny* question of who pays.
It's a *thorny* problem with no clean answer.

senses.gloss: Covered with sharp points that grow on a plant.
examples: Wear gloves — the branches are *thorny*.
A *thorny* hedge runs along the fence.

position: both — *a thorough search*; *she is thorough*
contrast: Don't mix it up with *through* /θruː/, which is a preposition, or with *though*. *Thorough* has two syllables: THUR-oh.

senses.gloss: Done carefully and completely, with nothing left out.
examples: The police did a *thorough* search of the building.
She's the most *thorough* editor I've worked with.
Give the pan a *thorough* cleaning before you use it.

position: both — *a thought-provoking film*; *the talk was thought-provoking*

senses.gloss: Making you think seriously about something.
examples: It's a *thought-provoking* documentary about food waste.
She asked a *thought-provoking* question at the end.
The talk was short but *thought-provoking*.

position: both — *a thoughtful gift*; *that was thoughtful of you*

senses.gloss: Kind, and careful about what other people need.
examples: That was a *thoughtful* gift.
It was *thoughtful* of you to call.
He's the most *thoughtful* person in the office.

senses.gloss: Careful and serious in thinking about something.
examples: She gave a *thoughtful* answer to a hard question.
The report is *thoughtful* and well argued.

senses.gloss: Looking as if you are deep in thought.
examples: He went quiet and *thoughtful* after the news.
There was a *thoughtful* look on her face.

position: both — *a thoughtless remark*; *it was thoughtless of him*

senses.gloss: Not thinking about how your words or actions affect other people.
examples: It was a *thoughtless* remark, but he didn't mean any harm.
Leaving the gate open was *thoughtless*.
She apologized for being *thoughtless* about the schedule.

position: both — *a threadbare rug*; *his coat was threadbare*
form: compound — *thread* + *bare*: worn until the threads show

senses.gloss: Worn so thin that the cloth is almost see-through.
examples: He still wears that *threadbare* corduroy jacket.
The rug by the door is *threadbare*.
The hotel towels were *threadbare*.

senses.gloss: Used so often that it no longer convinces anyone.
examples: That excuse is getting *threadbare*.
He repeated the same *threadbare* argument.

position: both — *a threatened species*; *he felt threatened*
contrast: *threatened* is how the person or animal feels; *threatening* is what causes the fear.

senses.gloss: In danger of being harmed or of dying out.
examples: The turtle is a *threatened* species in this state.
Small farms are *threatened* by rising costs.
Coastal towns are the most *threatened* by the storms.

senses.gloss: Feeling that someone may hurt you or take what is yours.
examples: He gets *threatened* by anyone younger than he is.
She said she felt *threatened* during the call.

position: both — *a threatening letter*; *his tone was threatening*
contrast: Compare *threatened*: *a threatening email* frightens people, *a threatened worker* is the one who is frightened.

senses.gloss: Suggesting that harm is coming.
examples: She got a *threatening* letter and called the police.
His tone turned *threatening*.
The dog took a *threatening* step toward the fence.

senses.gloss: Looking as if a storm is about to start.
examples: The sky looked *threatening* all afternoon.
*Threatening* clouds moved in over the lake.

position: both — *a three-dimensional model*; *the image is three-dimensional*

senses.gloss: Having height, width and depth, so it looks solid.
examples: The printer makes *three-dimensional* models out of plastic.
A globe is *three-dimensional*; a map is flat.
They built a *three-dimensional* map of the cave.

senses.gloss: Believable and fully developed, of a character in a story.
examples: The villain is the only *three-dimensional* character in the book.
She writes *three-dimensional* people, not types.

position: attributive only — *a three-legged stool*
contrast: The *-ed* here is a full syllable: *LEG-id*, not *legd*, like *ragged* and *naked*.

senses.gloss: Having three legs.
examples: He milked the cow on a *three-legged* stool.
Their *three-legged* dog gets around just fine.
The kids won the *three-legged* race at the picnic.

ru: состоящий из трёх предметов (о костюме, наборе)
position: attributive only — *a three-piece suit*

senses.gloss: Made up of three matching parts.
examples: He showed up in a *three-piece* suit.
They bought a *three-piece* luggage set.
The band is a *three-piece* outfit from Detroit.

position: attributive only — *a three-pronged approach*
form: compound — number + noun + *-ed*, from the *prongs* of a fork

senses.gloss: Working in three separate directions at the same time.
examples: The city announced a *three-pronged* approach to homelessness.
Their *three-pronged* strategy covers price, service and speed.
He led a *three-pronged* attack on the proposal.

position: attributive only — *a three-way race*

senses.gloss: Involving three people, groups or directions.
examples: It turned into a *three-way* race for mayor.
We set up a *three-way* call with the lawyer.
There's a *three-way* stop at the end of our street.

position: attributive only — *a threefold increase*
contrast: After a verb the same word is an adverb: *Enrollment grew threefold* — not *was threefold*.

senses.gloss: Three times as great, or made of three parts.
examples: The study found a *threefold* increase in risk.
Her job has a *threefold* purpose: teach, advise and recruit.
They expect a *threefold* rise in demand by spring.

position: both — *a thrifty shopper*; *my grandmother was thrifty*
contrast: *thrifty* is a compliment; *cheap* and *stingy* are insults for the same behavior.

senses.gloss: Careful with money and good at not wasting it.
examples: My grandmother was *thrifty* — she saved every jar.
*Thrifty* shoppers wait for the end-of-season sales.
He's *thriftier* than anyone I know, and he still travels.

position: attributive only — *a thriving business*
contrast: After a verb it is the verb, not the adjective: *Her business is thriving* is the present progressive.

senses.gloss: Growing well and doing very successfully.
examples: She runs a *thriving* bakery downtown.
The town has a *thriving* arts scene.
*Thriving* coral reefs are getting rare.

position: both — *a throaty laugh*; *her voice is throaty*

senses.gloss: Low and rough, made deep in the throat.
examples: She has a *throaty* laugh you can hear across the room.
The singer's voice gets *throatier* in the low notes.
The old truck has a *throaty* engine.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a throbbing headache*; *the pain was dull and throbbing*

senses.gloss: Hurting in a steady beat, like a pulse.
examples: I woke up with a *throbbing* headache.
There's a *throbbing* pain in my thumb where I hit it.
The ache was dull and *throbbing*, not sharp.

senses.gloss: Beating or sounding with a strong steady rhythm.
examples: *Throbbing* bass came through the wall all night.
We could hear the *throbbing* engines of the ferry.

position: attributive only — *a throwaway line*
form: compound from the phrasal verb *throw away*

senses.gloss: Meant to be thrown out after one use.
examples: The picnic came with *throwaway* plates and forks.
We live in a *throwaway* culture.
Cheap *throwaway* razors fill the shelf.

senses.gloss: Said quickly and without much thought, though people may still notice it.
examples: It was a *throwaway* line, but it made the whole room laugh.
His *throwaway* remark about the budget started a fight.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *thunderous applause*

senses.gloss: Extremely loud, like thunder.
examples: She left the stage to *thunderous* applause.
There was a *thunderous* crash as the shelf came down.
The crowd's roar was *thunderous*.

position: predicative only — *we were thunderstruck*

senses.gloss: So surprised that you cannot speak.
examples: We were *thunderstruck* when he said he was quitting.
She sat there *thunderstruck*, holding the letter.
The whole room looked *thunderstruck*.

position: both — *Tibetan monks*; *the script is Tibetan*
comparison: not gradable — but *very Tibetan* when it means 'typical of Tibet'
contrast: *Tibetan* is also a noun: a person from Tibet, and the language.

senses.gloss: From Tibet, or relating to Tibet and its people.
examples: The museum has a room of *Tibetan* art.
She studies *Tibetan* Buddhism.
The writing on the scroll is *Tibetan*.

position: both — *a ticklish situation*; *she's ticklish*

senses.gloss: Laughing and twitching when someone touches you lightly.
examples: Don't touch his feet — he's *ticklish*.
I'm *ticklish* on my sides.
The baby is *ticklish* under her chin.

senses.gloss: Needing careful handling because it could easily go wrong.
examples: Asking him about the money is a *ticklish* business.
The negotiation reached a *ticklish* stage.

position: attributive only — *a tidal pool*

senses.gloss: Relating to the daily rise and fall of the sea.
examples: The kids looked for crabs in the *tidal* pools.
A *tidal* creek runs behind the houses.
Scotland is testing *tidal* power turbines.

position: both — *a tied game*; *the score is tied*

senses.gloss: Level with the other side, with neither one ahead.
examples: The score is *tied* at two.
It was a *tied* game going into the ninth.
They're *tied* with Houston for first place.

senses.gloss: Fastened with a knot.
examples: His shoes weren't *tied*, and he tripped.
The bundle came in *tied* with string.

position: predicative only — *I'm tied up until four*
takes: *in* / *with* + noun — *tied up in meetings*, *tied up with a client*
contrast: Very common in American offices as a polite 'busy': *He's tied up right now* means he can't come to the phone.

senses.gloss: Too busy with something else to be available.
examples: I'm *tied up* until four — can we talk after that?
She's *tied up* in meetings all morning.
Sorry, he's *tied up* with a client right now.

senses.gloss: Held in something so that it cannot be used or moved.
examples: Most of their money is *tied up* in the house.
Traffic was *tied up* for two miles.

position: attributive only — *a tiered cake*
form: -ed from the noun *tier*, a level or row
contrast: *tiered* rhymes with *weird*, not with *tired* — one syllable.

senses.gloss: Built in levels, one above the other.
examples: They ordered a three-layer *tiered* cake.
The hall has *tiered* seating, so everyone can see.
We planted the slope in *tiered* beds.

senses.gloss: Organized in levels that give different amounts or prices.
examples: The company moved to *tiered* pricing.
It's a *tiered* system: basic, plus and premium.

position: both — *tight jeans*; *the lid is too tight*
contrast: *tight* is also an adverb after a verb (*Hold on tight*, *Sleep tight*), but before a participle use *tightly*: *tightly packed*.

senses.gloss: Fitting very closely to the body, often too closely.
examples: These jeans are too *tight*.
The shoes felt *tighter* after the hike.
He wore a *tight* black T-shirt.

senses.gloss: Firmly fixed and hard to move or undo.
examples: The lid is on too *tight*.
Make sure the knot is *tight*.

senses.gloss: Leaving very little room, time or money.
examples: We're working on a *tight* deadline.
Money is *tight* this month.
It's a *tight* schedule, but it can be done.

senses.gloss: Very close, with almost nothing between the sides.
examples: It was a *tight* game until the last minute.
The polls show a *tight* race.

position: attributive only — *a tight-fitting lid*

senses.gloss: Made to fit very closely, with no gap.
examples: Store the soup in a jar with a *tight-fitting* lid.
She wore a *tight-fitting* dress.
The mask needs a *tight-fitting* seal to work.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a tight-knit family*; *the team is tight-knit*

senses.gloss: Made of people who know each other well and help each other.
examples: They grew up in a *tight-knit* Italian neighborhood.
It's a *tight-knit* family — everyone shows up for everything.
The crew is *tight-knit* after three years together.

position: both — *a tightfisted landlord*; *he's tightfisted*
form: compound — *tight* + *fist* + *-ed*: holding the money in a closed hand
contrast: Always an insult, unlike *thrifty*, which is praise.

senses.gloss: Unwilling to spend or give money.
examples: Our landlord is *tightfisted* about repairs.
He's *tightfisted* with everyone but his grandkids.
The company has a *tightfisted* travel policy.

position: attributive only — *a time-honored tradition*
contrast: American spelling is *time-honored*; British writing has *time-honoured*.

senses.gloss: Respected because people have done it this way for a very long time.
examples: Opening day is a *time-honored* tradition here.
They settled it in the *time-honored* way, over coffee.
The recipe follows a *time-honored* method.

position: attributive only — *a time-release capsule*
form: compound — noun + noun used as one modifier
contrast: Labels also say *timed-release* and *extended-release* for the same thing.

senses.gloss: Made to let the medicine out slowly over several hours.
examples: The doctor switched him to a *time-release* capsule.
*Time-release* pain medication lasts through the night.
Some fertilizers use the same *time-release* idea.
